findings.finding: The stale classification proxy (oldest unpushed event ts < now − horizon) does not implement the ADR §5 condition it cites ('last convergence predates the N-day horizon'). The I5 argument runs the wrong way. Oldest-unpushed-ts being old implies stale, but a clone that last converged 60 days ago and wrote yesterday (push failed offline or against the rewritten remote) has a recent oldest unpushed event. It is classified fresh and its events are replayed, although ADR §5 says such a clone must be overridden.

findings.finding: The stale classification is a one-sided bound and diverges from ADR 0106 §5's criterion ('last convergence predates the N-day horizon'). The oldest unpushed event's ts is an UPPER bound on last convergence. So 'oldest unpushed < now−horizon' does imply stale, but 'oldest unpushed ≥ now−horizon' does not imply fresh. A clone offline for 60 days whose only writes happened yesterday is classified fresh and replays, although the ADR says it should be overridden.

findings.finding: The leaf redefines the parent's stale-clone criterion. The parent's C3 says a clone is stale when its 'last remote convergence is older than N days', and such a clone 'may NOT reintroduce' events and is reset with accepted loss. The leaf calls a clone stale only when 'its oldest unpushed event's ts is older than now − horizon_days'. An unpushed write can only happen after the last convergence, so its timestamp is at or after that convergence. The proxy therefore proves stale in one direction only: a clone that last converged more than N days ago but made its first offline write inside the horizon is classified fresh, and its local-only events are replayed onto the reclaimed remote. The parent says those must be discarded. Divergence kind on the divergent_implementation axis: a redefined parent deliverable (contradicts_reality as a definition). The uuid filter still keeps no-resurrection intact, so the practical impact is narrower than a safety break.

Unpushed-event ts is at best a one-sided bound on convergence time (an unpushed event is always newer than the last convergence). It does not tell you when the clone last fetched, and nothing in the leaf records a convergence watermark.
findings.finding: The leaf changes how the parent decides whether a clone is stale. The parent says a clone is stale when its LAST REMOTE CONVERGENCE is older than N days. The leaf uses a different test: the clone is stale when its OLDEST UNPUSHED EVENT's ts is older than the horizon, and then it decides once for the whole clone (replay everything or discard everything). This disagrees with the parent's guarantee for live clones. A clone that converged recently but still holds one old unpushed event (for example, a push that kept failing) is called stale and loses ALL of its unpushed work, including events written inside the horizon. A clone whose last convergence is older than N days but whose only unpushed writes are recent is called fresh and keeps its work. Divergence kind: redefines a parent deliverable (contradicts_reality candidate), unless the parent is updated to adopt the proxy.

findings.finding: The stale-classification rule rests on the claim 'Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.' The repo contradicts this. `sync.push` has a supported `off` mode, so writes do not always auto-push. Async pushes are best-effort. Reconverge (fetch, then adopt or merge) never pushes, so a clone can converge daily while still holding unpushed events. Also, concurrency.md's I5 is 'Single locked write path', not the auto-push invariant. So the age of the oldest unpushed event does not bound when the clone last converged. Under the plan's rule, a recently converged clone (`sync.push=off`, or one whose pushes keep failing) is classified stale and its unpushed work is discarded. ADR 0106 §5 accepts that loss only for clones whose LAST CONVERGENCE predates the horizon.
findings.location: Approach §2 'Stale vs fresh' (and the matching docs/concurrency.md step 2 text)
scenarios: A clone with `sync.push=off` (or `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off`) fetches and reconverges every minute but has held local events for 40 days. After the reclaim swap it is classified stale and all its unpushed events are discarded, even though it last converged moments before the swap.

With `sync.push=async`, a clone's detached pushes fail silently (stdout/stderr go to DEVNULL) for longer than N days while its reads keep reconverging. It is misclassified as stale, and its work survives only in the local-only backup ref.
findings.suggested_fix: Base 'stale' on a direct last-convergence signal, as ADR §5 describes. Options: the committer date of the newest commit HEAD shares with what it last fetched, or a timestamp recorded per clone on each successful reconverge. Alternatively, keep the event-age proxy but state its limits, never discard events from a `sync.push=off` clone (back up and replay instead), and add a test for that case. Change the citation from I5 to the auto-push statement at concurrency.md:576.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the fresh-clone override crash-atomic: build the replay commit before moving HEAD and switch with a single ref update, or detect and resume an un-replayed backup ref on the next reconverge; add a test that interrupts between reset and replay.

The write lock serialises concurrent writers but does not make the reset+replay sequence crash-atomic; no recovery or resume step is described.
findings.finding: The override is a multi-step, non-atomic mutation: backup ref, then `reset --hard` to the remote, then a separate replay commit. If the process dies or errors after the reset and before the replay commit, the fresh clone's unpushed events vanish from the working tree. They survive only in the backup ref, and no WARNING is logged, because the fresh path never logs. On retry, HEAD now shares a merge-base with the remote, so `_do_reconverge` takes the normal path. The override, and therefore the replay, is never re-entered. The operation is not idempotent under retry.
findings.location: Approach steps 3–4 ("Point refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp> at the old local HEAD ..., then reset --hard to the pinned remote commit" / "re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit")
scenarios: A fresh clone is killed (laptop sleep, SIGTERM, disk-full on commit) between the reset and the replay commit. Its recent writes silently disappear, and the next sync sees an ordinary fast-forwardable clone.
The replay commit fails on a git error. The clone is left at the remote tip with fresh writes discarded and no WARNING.
findings.suggested_fix: Construct the replay commit with plumbing before touching HEAD: take the remote tree plus the unpushed event blobs, write the tree with `git write-tree`/`commit-tree`, and parent it on the remote commit. Then write the backup ref and move the branch with one `update-ref`, followed by a working-tree checkout. Alternatively, on every reconverge, scan `refs/rebar/stale-override/*` for backups whose unpushed fresh events are absent from HEAD and replay them.

The plan defines no retirement path: no expiry, no GC, and no documented manual cleanup. Each ref keeps the full reclaimed history reachable locally. On a clone, that defeats the purpose of reclamation, and the refs accumulate across successive epochs.

findings.finding: The lineage proof does not prove the remote is a rewrite of THIS store when the local epoch is the pre-epoch `null`. Today every store is pre-epoch, so the first reclaim of ANY store stamps `epoch_lineage: [null]`. Any un-epoched local clone whose HEAD shares no history with such a remote is then judged 'superseded' and reset onto it. That makes an unrelated store (for example a misconfigured `sync.remote`, or another project's reclaimed tickets remote) look like a successor, which undoes the plan's promise that unrelated stores keep today's refusal.

findings.finding: Deciding 'unpushed' as 'uuid appears nowhere on the remote tip, as a file or in a remote SNAPSHOT's `source_event_uuids`' is not stable under the program's companion retired-event GC. A re-compaction's SNAPSHOT deliberately does not cite events folded by the earlier SNAPSHOT. So once the remote GCs `.retired` files, events that were pushed long ago (and that a converged clone still holds as `.retired`) are no longer known to the remote by either test. They then count as unpushed. On a fresh clone they are replayed live with the suffix stripped, which is a resurrection. Because their timestamps are old, they also make an otherwise fresh clone count as stale, so its genuinely recent writes are thrown away.

A clone whose pushes kept failing (e.g. credentials) while fetches succeeded holds one long-unpushed event. It gets classified stale even though it converged recently.

findings.finding: The override is not atomic, and the plan says nothing about a failure partway through. Step 3 resets HEAD to the remote, and only then does step 4 stage and commit the replay. If the replay fails after the reset (update-index, checkout or commit), the clone sits on the remote tip with a half-staged index. On the next reconverge the histories are related with nothing local ahead, so the existing ff-adopt `reset --hard` quietly wipes the staged replay. The events then survive only in a backup ref the operator has not been told holds them.
findings.location: Approach steps 3–4 ('Backup, then override' / 'Fresh clones replay')
scenarios: `git commit` fails (hook environment, disk full, identity config) after the reset. The next sync round's ff-adopt removes the staged event files, and the fresh clone's unpushed work is lost without a stale-style WARNING.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the final commit before touching HEAD. With GIT_INDEX_FILE pointing at a temp file: `read-tree <remote>`, then `update-index --add --cacheinfo 100644,<blob>,<live_path>` for each replayed event, `write-tree`, `commit-tree <tree> -p <remote> -m ...`. Then `update-ref` the backup and run a single `reset --hard <new-commit>`. If any step before the reset fails, HEAD is unchanged and the DIVERGED-style warning is logged.

findings.finding: Both unpushed-event detection and stale classification silently depend on a contract with S2's not-yet-built publish-swap: every reclaimed event uuid must remain visible on the rewritten remote, either as a file or in some SNAPSHOT's `source_event_uuids`. If S2 drops reclaimed events without that trace (e.g. removes whole reclaimed tickets), every normally-synced clone still holds those old pushed events locally. They then count as 'unpushed' and are older than the horizon. Every clone, including fresh ones, would then be classified stale and have its genuinely fresh writes discarded. The plan neither states this contract for S2 nor tests against a realistic collapsed baseline.

findings.finding: A 'fresh' replay that re-adds the original file byte for byte does not actually deliver events whose timestamp prefix is older than the remote's latest SNAPSHOT for that ticket. The reducer skips every event whose index comes before the latest SNAPSHOT. So an unpushed event written before a remote compaction of the same ticket is committed and pushed but never takes effect. Reclamation requires below-horizon events to be folded first, so remote compactions shortly before a swap are the expected case. Yet the plan counts these events as 'replayed', not discarded, and logs no warning.
